column1: # The preference keys that defaults.sh (make defaults) writes, in the order it
# writes them. Before it changes a key, it records the value the key had in
# ~/.mrk/defaults-rollback.sh, so the change can be undone. Its --check
# compares each line with this Mac and changes nothing. MRK-1, the defaults
# reference, shows each key with its description from docs/defaults/script.js,
# and check-defaults-desc fails when a key has none.
# One key on each line: six fields, separated by tabs.
#   domain   the defaults domain: NSGlobalDomain, or the bundle id of an app
#   type     bool, int, float or string
#   value    true or false for a bool, a whole number for an int, a number
#            such as 0.5 for a float, and any text for a string. A string that
#            starts with ~/ is a path in your home directory.
#            trackpad: only with --with-trackpad, as make trackpad runs it.
#            existing: only when the domain exists. A sandboxed app, such as
#            Mail or TextEdit, keeps its preferences in its container, and
#            makes them when it is set up or first used. Before that, defaults
#            write fails for Mail, and for TextEdit it writes a file outside
#            the container that TextEdit never reads. Run make defaults again
#            after you set up the app.
#   section  the heading that MRK-1 shows the key under
# In a field, a backslash starts an escape: \t is a tab, \n is a newline and \\
# is a backslash. A space and a quote need no escape. A line that starts with #
# is a comment, and an empty line is ignored. defaults.sh refuses the file,
# before it writes anything, when a line is not one key or when two lines have
# The same key, type and value in two domains of one section is one setting:
# MRK-1 shows it once, and check-defaults-desc wants one description, for the
# first of the domains. The trackpad keys are like this.
# - Software Update and the App Store. softwareupdated reads its settings from
#   /Library/Preferences, not from your domain, so a key here changes nothing.
#   A write to the system domain turns automatic downloads back on, and they
#   were turned off on 2026-09-15 to stop a macOS 27 download. Audit 15, T-3.
# - Music. Music's own Settings keep its preferences. The System Policy of
#   macOS 26 stops any other process writing com.apple.Music, so on a new Mac
#   the writes fail on every run. Full Disk Access does not change that, and
#   neither does opening Music first. Audit 11, R-1.
